# The cookbook

The 1446 book ends its explanations with a list: ninety-four everyday
words, written out in the new letters. Persimmon, ice, tiger, star. It shows
usage, not rules: the new letters could spell the words of daily life.

You have now met every word of gog, and every way of joining them into a
sentence. What is left is practice on real questions. This part is gog's
version of the 1446 list. It is organized by your columns and your question, because you know
those before you know a chart's name. You will not find a chapter called
"Histograms". You will find a recipe called *How is a measurement
distributed?*, and the sentence that answers it. (If you already know the
chart's name, the [chart names appendix](../chart-names.qmd) translates it into
a sentence.)

The recipes use the book's shared tables, which you can download from [The
book's data](../book-data.qmd). Each recipe chapter shows the first rows of every
shared table before drawing from it. The recipes use only atoms taught in Parts
I to III, and most link back to the chapters that own their atoms.

Almost every recipe has the same shape: the question, the sentence that answers
it, the plot, and a line or two on why it works. Many then show what is one atom
away: the same sentence with one small change, such as an atom swapped or one
of its arguments changed. That is the real lesson. A cookbook of finished charts
teaches you charts. This one teaches you that the recipes are connected: swap
one atom in a recipe and you have another.
